title: Woods v. Interstate Realty Co. (1949)
summary: The corporation could not use diversity jurisdiction to evade the state restriction on suits by a corporation that had failed to qualify locally.
notes:
This is the Interstate Realty case, not Burlington Northern v. Woods. Later readings ask how an asserted federal rule or federal policy changes the analysis.

Interstate Realty, a Tennessee corporation, sued a Mississippi resident for a broker's commission on the sale of Mississippi land while doing business in Mississippi without qualifying under its statute.

sections.Parties: An out-of-state corporation sought to enforce a claim in federal court in Mississippi.
sections.Material Facts: The corporation had not complied with the state’s registration or qualification requirements. State law consequently barred the relevant action in its own courts. The plaintiff sought to proceed in the federal diversity forum despite that restriction.
sections.Procedural History: The district court granted summary judgment for the defendant and dismissed with prejudice, holding the contract void under Mississippi law. The Fifth Circuit reversed, reading Mississippi law as making the contract merely unenforceable in Mississippi courts rather than void. The Supreme Court (Douglas, J., 6–3) reversed the Fifth Circuit, holding that under Erie the summary judgment was properly granted.
sections.Issue: Could a federal diversity forum enforce the claim when the state courts would deny the unqualified corporation that remedy?
sections.Holding: No. The state limitation on enforcement applied.
sections.Reasoning: Allowing the corporation to proceed only because it could invoke diversity would produce the type of unequal administration Erie sought to avoid. The federal forum supplied a tribunal, not a general enlargement of the plaintiff’s state-law rights.

learning.why: The corporation could not use diversity jurisdiction to evade the state restriction on suits by a corporation that had failed to qualify locally.

topics.cp-erie-outcome: The corporation could not obtain in federal diversity court the enforcement barred by the state’s door-closing rule.
topics.cp-forum-shopping: Federal access did not confer a greater state-law entitlement on the unqualified out-of-state corporation.
topics.cp-erie: Woods extends Erie and Guaranty Trust to a state door-closing statute, holding that a party barred in state court is likewise barred in federal court.
topics.cp-diversity: The case limits what a plaintiff can gain by invoking diversity jurisdiction against a state rule barring suit.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Jackson, joined by Justices Rutledge and Burton, dissented, arguing that the Court's refusal to accept the state court's own reading of the effect of its statute (unenforceable in state court, not void) was a perversion of the Erie doctrine.
